/Through Saturday/...
Issued at 1204 AM MDT Sun Nov 1 2026

Current satellite imagery shows some mid-level clouds as well as 
some patchy fog in Morgan County, eastern Elbert County, and 
northern Lincoln County. Areas of dense fog or low stratus look 
possible once again through this morning for northern Colorado and
along/near the Palmer Divide. This fog could make it as far south
as the northern Denver metro and east to DIA. Still some 
questions about how widespread and/or dense the fog will be...A 
Dense Fog Advisory may be needed later this morning if confidence 
increases through the overnight. Otherwise, lows tonight will stay
in the 40s in the plains and 20s and 30s for the high country.

Sunday will be another nice afternoon with high temperatures in 
the 60s for the plains, but there will be more clouds compared to 
Saturday. Some wind gusts of 20-30 mph are possible in the 
afternoon mainly across the eastern plains. Southwest flow aloft 
through at least Monday midday continues to bring rich moisture to
our area. The trough to our west looks to move rather quickly 
from the Great Basin on Sunday afternoon to eastern Colorado by 
Monday evening. A low looks to form in southeast Colorado on 
Monday evening, but the strongest energy continues moving off to 
the northeast. At the surface, a cold front is progged to move 
through early on Monday morning and make it through our southeast 
counties by Monday afternoon. Therefore, temperatures on Monday 
afternoon do not look to warm up very much from the low 50s and 
possible even falling into the upper 40s on the plains. Have 
nudged Monday afternoon temperatures down based on the latest 
short-term guidance. Monday afternoon also looks windy for most of
the plains with some gusts of 30-40 mph and isolated wind gusts 
up to 50 mph. Only slightly lower wind gusts are still possible 
through Tuesday for the eastern plains.

In terms of precipitation: Light rain/snow showers should move 
into the high country on Sunday afternoon with widely scattered 
light rain showers by the evening for the plains given the 
unfavorable southwest flow aloft initially. Snow levels look to 
start rather high on Sunday afternoon (> 12,000 ft) and then 
quickly drop by Sunday evening into the overnight to around 10,000
feet. We expect a further decrease in snow levels to 8,500 to 
9,000 feet by Monday afternoon. Therefore, snow becomes 
increasingly likely above about 8,500 to 9,000 ft for late Sunday,
through Monday, and lingering into early Tuesday morning. The 
northern mountains look most favored for the higher snowfall 
amounts in our area. Given the current snowfall forecasts and 
limited scope of the heaviest totals, we have held off on issuing 
a Winter Weather Advisory. One may be needed in a future forecast 
package. The north flow behind the front introduces an upslope 
component for the Palmer Divide where QPF could be maximized on 
Monday evening. As we get into Monday night and early Tuesday 
morning, colder air continues to filter in, so snow levels could 
drop low enough (down to about 7,000-7,500 ft) for a few flakes on
the Palmer Divide. No snow accumulation is expected there given 
the decreasing precipitation chances. Overall, we have slightly 
increased QPF from the previous forecast for the next 48-60 hours 
for locations in the high country and Palmer Divide. 

Some ridging moves in for Tuesday with temperatures rebounding 
into the upper 50s to low 60s for the plains. Another trough moves
through on Wednesday with another round of precipitation possible
though the signal for this remains murky. Some snow looks 
possible again for the high country with rain showers possibly 
spilling onto the plains once again. At this time, have low PoPs 
for this potential starting Wednesday evening.

Once this system moves through, northwest flow aloft looks to 
hold for Thursday and Friday keeping highs in the upper 50s to low
60s for the plains. Another cold front is possible as we get to 
the weekend with unsettled weather looking to return as well.
